content.markdown:
# Reducing Serbian support-search misses without full re-indexing

## Verified facts
- LinguaBot attributes search failures to Serbian inflection and mixed scripts, including script changes inside words. [F1]
- The company reports that about 18% of 12,000 real support queries from one bank returned no useful result. Its separate labelled query-response dataset contains around 85,000 pairs across all clients. [F2]
- LinguaBot currently uses Elasticsearch with a Croatian-oriented stemmer. It reports that manual synonym-list maintenance does not scale as clients introduce product terminology quarterly. [F3]
- The company identifies approximately EUR 8,000 for tooling or data work and says its two in-house linguists can annotate or validate solutions. [F4]
- Nikolić’s work presents Serbian-specific hybrid lemmatization, within-token script normalization, and retrieval comparisons in which full lemmatization with paradigm-aware indexing achieved the highest F1. [F5]
- Her lexicon research reports lower paradigm correctness for borrowings than common vocabulary. Her normalization study reports a tradeoff: lookup tables had highest precision, while the neural model generalized better to unseen borrowings. [F6]
- Nikolić’s participation material lists openness to joint projects. [F7]

## Potential benefits
- For the company: The experiment could identify which linguistic components reduce actual support-search misses and whether the best configuration can meet the bank-specific target while accommodating vocabulary changes without full re-indexing.
- For the researcher: Subject to agreement and permissions, Nikolić could test how corpus-derived morphology and cross-script methods transfer to support retrieval, using labelled queries and expert-reviewed product-vocabulary cases.

## Our inference
- This suggests a strong methodological match, but corpus and social-media results do not establish useful-answer retrieval performance on banking or telecom support, especially mixed-script typos and unseen products.
- Query-time normalization and paradigm expansion could support vocabulary updates without rebuilding the index, but compatibility with existing indexed representations remains untested. Borrowing errors and normalization-induced ambiguity could increase irrelevant results.
- This joint-project proposal is conditional because Nikolić’s availability is unknown; openness to collaboration does not establish a delivery commitment.

## Proposed next steps
- First, propose replaying company-labelled queries against corresponding knowledge-base snapshots. Reserve separate tuning and held-out evaluation samples; check duplicate, client and temporal leakage. Independently switch Serbian lemmatization, within-token script normalization and paradigm expansion on/off: test the current Elasticsearch baseline, each alone, all pairs and all three, holding other settings constant. Select the best configuration on tuning data, then freeze it. Measure no-useful-result query events divided by all evaluated query events, counting repeated submissions separately without merging. Linguists would adjudicate every evaluation query at an agreed retrieval depth; unresolved cases count as misses. Require the upper 95% confidence bound below 5%, separately on held-out queries from the original bank; pooled results cannot substitute. Report other clients and mixed-script, inflectional and unseen-product subsets separately. Insufficient bank data means no pass. Nikolić would propose linguistic components; company engineers would implement replay and integration, with linguists validating relevance. Go/no-go also requires the feasibility and maintenance gates below, regardless of which configuration wins.
- Test new product vocabulary through query-time or auxiliary-lexicon updates in the existing Elasticsearch workflow, with zero full re-index operations as a gate. Repeat held-out retrieval evaluation after updates. Before testing, agree precision, latency and linguist-hours-per-update limits; measure each and require compliance alongside the miss-rate gate. Bound annotation work within the two linguists’ agreed allocation. Investigate null component effects and interactions rather than treating a null effect alone as disproving the mechanism.
- Propose month one for permissions, baseline reproduction and evaluation definitions; months two–four for component comparisons and integration; months five–six for frozen evaluation and update rehearsal. Gate continuation on a testable prototype within six months and tooling/data costs within approximately EUR 8,000. Research-time funding, engineering allocation and maintenance ownership remain to be agreed; these are proposed planning limits, not commitments.

## Open questions
- Can Nikolić confirm availability for this joint project and agree research responsibilities with the company’s engineering and maintenance owners?
- What client permissions, de-identification rules, processing-location restrictions and commercial-use licences would govern the datasets, knowledge-base snapshots and research tools?
- Can the company supply independent held-out data from the original bank and agree useful-result depth, relevance adjudication, precision, latency and maintenance-effort acceptance limits?
- Which Elasticsearch mappings, permitted incremental-update mechanisms, compute resources, staff allocations and research-time funding are available?
